stories.headline: SC hears pleas on SIR as deleted voters face detention risk
stories.summary: The Supreme Court is hearing a batch of petitions challenging the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, including one filed by INDIA bloc leaders led by Rahul Gandhi. In its October 26 affidavit, the Election Commission of India denied any difference of opinion between the Chief Election Commissioner and the Election Commissioners over the SIR process, a claim Rahul Gandhi told the Court is unsupported by proof. Separately, the ECI assured the Court that voters deleted during SIR who file Form 6 to restore their names will not face prosecution. Ground reports from West Bengal describe voters who say they can neither effectively appeal their deletion nor vote, while Reuters reported that some Muslims removed from the rolls face detention and deportation proceedings. TheWire.in has questioned gaps between the ECI's own records and its public explanations of the Bengal revision.
stories.whyItMatters: The case tests the scope of the ECI's powers under Article 324, the procedural safeguards in electoral roll revision, and the constitutional right to vote — a recurring theme for GS-II polity and governance questions.

perspectives.take: Frames the story around constitutional accountability — Rahul Gandhi's argument that the ECI has produced no proof that the SIR was a unanimous decision of the CEC and the Election Commissioners.

static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power of courts to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 (SC) and 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction.

static.topic: Election Commission of India and Electoral Roll Revision (SIR)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Constitutional Bodies & Elections
static.whatIsIt: The ECI, under Article 324, has superintendence, direction and control of elections, including the preparation and revision of electoral rolls. A Special Intensive Revision (SIR) is a door-to-door, intensive revision of the rolls rather than the routine annual revision.
static.background: The ECI was established on 25 January 1950 and has functioned as a multi-member body (CEC plus two Election Commissioners) since 1993; appointments are now governed by the CEC and Other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. Rolls are prepared under the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, with SIR conducted under Section 22 of the 1950 Act. Form 6 is used to apply for inclusion of a name, Form 7 to object, and Form 8 for corrections.
static.geography: West Bengal is among the states where the SIR has been carried out, alongside other poll-bound states.
static.socioEconomic: Deletion from the rolls can affect political representation and, in practice, create difficulties in accessing welfare and documentation that rely on identity and residence proof.
static.whyInNews: The ECI told the Supreme Court that no prosecution will be initiated against SIR-deleted voters who file Form 6 to restore their names, even as petitions challenge the revision process itself.
static.wayForward: Transparent publication of the reasons for deletion, accessible and time-bound claims-and-objections and appeal mechanisms, and clear communication on the legal consequences of deletion.
prelimsPointers: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections, including preparation of electoral rolls, in the ECI.
SIR is conducted under Section 22 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950; Form 6 is the application for inclusion of a name in the electoral roll.
Article 326 provides for elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies on the basis of adult suffrage.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether the ECI's powers under Article 324 and the RP Act, 1950 strike the right balance between electoral integrity and the citizen's right to vote.

static.topic: Citizenship, Detention and Deportation
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Citizenship & Fundamental Rights
static.whatIsIt: Citizenship is governed by the Citizenship Act, 1955, while the Foreigners Act, 1946 governs the detention and expulsion of foreigners. Foreigners Tribunals adjudicate disputed citizenship claims in certain states.
static.background: Articles 5 to 11 of the Constitution deal with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution and empower Parliament to regulate it. The Citizenship Act, 1955 has been amended in 1986, 2003 and 2019. The Foreigners (Tribunals) Order, 1964 provides the tribunal framework, and the National Register of Citizens exercise was completed in Assam in 2019.
static.geography: West Bengal and Assam, as border states, are the principal theatres of citizenship-verification and detention proceedings.
static.socioEconomic: Risk of statelessness, detention, loss of livelihood and legal costs fall disproportionately on poor and minority households.
static.whyInNews: Reuters reported that some Muslims deleted from India's voter rolls face detention and deportation proceedings, linking roll revision to citizenship status questions.
static.wayForward: Strict adherence to due process, access to legal aid, and clarity on whether and how deletion from an electoral roll bears on citizenship determination.
prelimsPointers: The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides for acquisition and termination of citizenship.
Under the Foreigners Act, 1946, a 'foreigner' means a person who is not a citizen of India.

stories.headline: COP31 draft urges 1.5°C goal as climate finance gap persists
stories.summary: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, is midway through negotiations, with a draft agreement urging countries to work to get back to the 1.5°C target and accelerate action to exit fossil fuels. However, the talks are overshadowed by a persistent climate finance gap, as Western governments' political attention has shifted to US elections, the Iran war, the Ukraine war, and security and inflationary pressures. Developing countries are calling on developed nations to lead both emissions cuts and finance efforts, while civil society groups have taken their demands beyond emissions in street protests. For India, a report presented at COP31 suggests faster electrification could cut the fossil fuel import bill by over 40% to ₹7.4 lakh crore by FY35, with electricity meeting 54% of energy demand and transport offering the largest substitution opportunity.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi, Putin summit in Shenzhen; Quad leaders meet in Manila
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump is on an Asia trip that has produced deals in Manila and is set to culminate in a three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, where Trump has said he will raise Russia's war in Ukraine. US officials have indicated the agenda also covers West Asia and the stability of global energy supplies, along with nuclear arms control, while Beijing has hailed the gathering as being of 'groundbreaking significance'. Quad leaders met in Manila on the eve of the talks, a move read as a signal to China that the grouping remains active even as Washington engages Beijing and Moscow directly. Commentators are divided on whether the summit amounts to a 'Yalta 2.0' — a great-power carve-up of spheres of influence — or, as sceptics argue, a largely symbolic exercise with limited deliverables.
stories.whyItMatters: Summitry of this kind tests the rules-based order and India's multi-alignment: New Delhi must protect its Quad, Russia and Global South equities without being reduced to a bystander in decisions taken over its head. It feeds directly into GS-II questions on strategic autonomy, minilateralism and UNSC reform.

static.topic: India's Strategic Autonomy in a Great-Power Summitry Moment
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & the World; effect of policies of major powers on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks, engaging simultaneously across the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and the Quad (with the US, Japan and Australia) gained salience after 2017.
static.whyInNews: Quad leaders met in Manila just before a US-China-Russia summit in Shenzhen, testing whether India can hold its Quad, Russia and Global South equities together while Washington, Beijing and Moscow negotiate directly.
static.wayForward: Sustain multi-alignment by deepening Quad deliverables without converting it into a military alliance, retaining independent Russia ties, and using BRICS/SCO and the Global South platform to avoid being a rule-taker in great-power bargains.

SCO: India and Pakistan joined in 2017.

static.topic: P5 Summity and the Case for UNSC Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance; important international institutions
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion. Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: A US-China-Russia summit revives the concern that global outcomes are being settled by the P5 outside UN processes, sharpening the case for a more representative Security Council and for India's permanent seat.
static.wayForward: Push for text-based negotiations in the IGN, build coalitions with the G4, African and Latin American groups, and press for veto restraint in mass-atrocity situations.

static.mainsAngle: India's claim rests on representativeness, population and contributions; assess the obstacles — veto politics and the Africa group's Ezulwini Consensus.

static.topic: Nuclear Arms Control and Strategic Stability
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — disarmament and nuclear diplomacy
static.whatIsIt: The global nuclear architecture rests on the NPT (1968, in force 1970), which recognises five nuclear-weapon states, and the CTBT (1996), which has not entered into force. US-Russia bilateral limits have been carried by New START (2010), extended in 2021 to February 2026.
static.background: India is not a party to the NPT or the CTBT, tested in 1974 and 1998, and follows credible minimum deterrence with a no-first-use posture. It joined the MTCR (2016), Wassenaar Arrangement (2017) and Australia Group (2018); NSG membership remains pending.
static.whyInNews: US officials have indicated nuclear arms control is on the agenda of the Shenzhen meeting, at a moment when the last major US-Russia arms-control treaty is nearing expiry.
static.wayForward: India should press for strategic stability dialogue among major powers, guard against arms-racing spillovers into Asia, and continue seeking NSG membership as a responsible nuclear state.
prelimsPointers: NPT recognises five nuclear-weapon states: US, Russia, UK, France, China.
CTBT has not entered into force; India, Pakistan and North Korea have not signed it.
India is a member of the MTCR, Wassenaar Arrangement and Australia Group, but not the NSG.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether plurilateral great-power arms-control bargains can substitute for inclusive, treaty-based disarmament frameworks that include India.

stories.summary: The Delhi government is in talks with the World Bank to design an airshed-based pollution-control strategy that would coordinate action with neighbouring states, moving away from city-only curbs towards targeted regional measures. static.topic: Airshed-based air pollution governance and cooperative federalism
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Centre-State Relations
static.whatIsIt: An 'airshed' is a geographic basin within which air pollutants circulate and interact, so its boundaries rarely match municipal or state borders. Airshed management therefore means coordinating pollution-control policy across all states and cities sharing the same air basin, instead of city-by-city emergency curbs.
static.background: India's quasi-federal scheme divides powers through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists in the Seventh Schedule, with residuary powers with the Union (Article 248). Public health and sanitation is a State List subject, which is why the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 was enacted using Article 252 (consent of states) rather than ordinary Union legislative competence. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) examined Centre-State balance, and the Inter-State Council (Article 263) exists as a recommendatory coordination and dispute-resolution body. Environmental coordination across states has historically run through the Central Pollution Control Board and, for the capital region, through bodies created on Supreme Court directions.
static.geography: The Delhi–NCR airshed extends beyond the National Capital Territory into NCR districts of Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and adjoining parts of Rajasthan, with episodic contributions from Punjab and Haryana during the post-monsoon stubble-burning window.
static.socioEconomic: Air pollution imposes a health burden concentrated on outdoor workers, the elderly, children and patients with respiratory illness, and its costs spill across state boundaries — the source states of emissions do not bear the full cost of the pollution they generate, which is the classic inter-jurisdictional externality that an airshed framework tries to internalise.
static.whyInNews: The Delhi government is in talks with the World Bank on an airshed-based pollution-control strategy coordinating with neighbouring states, as reported by Mint.
static.wayForward: Give the airshed body a clear statutory mandate, a shared emissions inventory and common monitoring standards; use the Inter-State Council or a dedicated NCR-plus platform for binding coordination; and pair regional targets with fiscal transfers so that states bearing abatement costs are compensated.
prelimsPointers: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 was enacted under Article 252 because air pollution was then a State List subject.
The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted under Article 253 to implement decisions of the Stockholm Conference.
The Inter-State Council under Article 263 is a recommendatory body; it cannot bind states.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how far India's federal architecture permits binding, region-wide environmental regulation, and assess whether an airshed authority would strengthen or strain cooperative federalism.

static.topic: Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) and the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP)
static.syllabusNode: Environment & Ecology — Pollution and Environmental Governance
static.whatIsIt: CAQM is a statutory body for the National Capital Region and adjoining areas, empowered to coordinate, direct and enforce air quality measures across the concerned states. GRAP is its graded set of emergency measures that tighten in stages as air quality deteriorates, covering construction, transport, industry and waste burning.
static.background: The Supreme Court's directions in the long-running M.C. Mehta air pollution litigation led to the creation of the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA) in 1998 and to the first Graded Response Action Plan, notified in the mid-2010s and implemented from 2017. Parliament replaced EPCA with CAQM through the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021, which gave the commission statutory backing and powers to issue binding directions. GRAP was subsequently revised into a four-stage structure with pre-defined AQI triggers.
static.geography: Operates over Delhi and the NCR districts of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, with coordination reaching into Punjab and Haryana for stubble-burning periods.
static.socioEconomic: GRAP restrictions fall unevenly — construction workers, transport operators and small industry bear immediate livelihood costs while the health benefits are diffuse, making compensation and sequencing politically contested.
static.whyInNews: Delhi's air quality was reported in the 'poor' category with Stage III GRAP curbs continuing, even as the city opened talks on a longer-term airshed strategy.
static.wayForward: Shift from episodic emergency measures to a year-round action calendar with pre-committed funding for dust control, mechanised road sweeping and clean-fuel transitions, so that restrictions are not the only tool available.
prelimsPointers: GRAP has four stages tied to AQI thresholds — Stage I (Poor, 201–300), Stage II (Very Poor, 301–400), Stage III (Severe, 401–450) and Stage IV (Severe Plus, 451–500).
The National Air Quality Index has six categories: Good, Satisfactory, Moderate, Poor, Very Poor and Severe.
CAQM is a statutory body created by an Act of Parliament in 2021, replacing the Supreme Court-constituted EPCA.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether graded emergency action plans address the structural drivers of winter air pollution or merely manage its worst episodes.

static.topic: National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) and urban air quality management
static.syllabusNode: Environment & Ecology — Air Pollution Policy and Institutions
static.whatIsIt: NCAP is the Union government's framework for reducing ambient particulate pollution in identified cities through city-specific action plans, monitoring expansion and capacity support to municipal bodies.
static.background: Launched by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in January 2019, NCAP initially targeted a 20–30 per cent reduction in PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations by 2024 against a 2017 base year, and this was later revised upward to a 40 per cent reduction by 2025–26. It began with a set of non-attainment cities — those exceeding national ambient air quality standards — and the list was subsequently expanded to cover more cities, including million-plus urban centres. Implementation relies on state pollution control boards and municipal corporations, with the Fifteenth Finance Commission also earmarking air quality grants for million-plus cities.
static.geography: National in scope, with city action plans concentrated in Indo-Gangetic Plain cities where meteorological conditions trap pollutants during winter.
static.socioEconomic: Urban air pollution links to transport and energy access, informal-sector exposure, and the livelihood costs of restrictions, making it as much an urban governance and equity question as a technical one.
static.whyInNews: The airshed discussions with the World Bank raise the question of how a regional approach would sit alongside NCAP's city-level architecture.
static.wayForward: Align NCAP city targets with airshed-level emission inventories, publish verifiable annual progress data, and build municipal capacity for continuous monitoring and enforcement.
prelimsPointers: NCAP was launched in January 2019 by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
Its reduction target was revised to 40 per cent for PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations by 2025–26.
NCAP operates through city-specific action plans for non-attainment cities, implemented by state boards and municipal bodies.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss why India's urban air quality programmes have struggled to deliver measurable reductions, and suggest institutional reforms.

prelims: The National Air Quality Index has six categories — Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderate (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very Poor (301–400) and Severe (401–500); Delhi's reported reading of 216 falls in the 'poor' band.
GRAP is a graded emergency action plan with four AQI-triggered stages for Delhi-NCR, administered by the statutory Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM Act, 2021).

The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 was enacted under Article 252 as air pollution was then a State List subject, while the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 used Article 253 to implement international commitments.

An 'airshed' is the geographic basin within which pollutants circulate; the Delhi–NCR airshed extends into Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, with episodic contributions from stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana.
stories.mainsQuestion: The airshed approach shifts air quality governance from city-centric curbs to regional coordination. Examine the institutional, federal and fiscal challenges in operationalising airshed-level pollution management in India, and suggest a workable framework.

stories.headline: Cyclone Akvan nears Andhra coast as Kutch marks 25 years of quake rebuilding
stories.summary: The India Meteorological Department has forecast that Cyclone Akvan over the Bay of Bengal will intensify into a 'very severe' cyclonic storm and approach the Andhra Pradesh coast around 20 November, with fishermen advised not to venture into the sea. It is the third cyclone threat to Andhra Pradesh in three weeks. The Regional Meteorological Centre, Chennai, expects only light rainfall over parts of coastal Tamil Nadu on 17 November, with mainly dry weather over the rest of the state. Separately, the 25th anniversary of the 2001 Kutch earthquake has revived discussion of that reconstruction effort as a template for crisis response and rebuilding.
stories.whyItMatters: Cyclone forecasting, coastal vulnerability and post-disaster reconstruction are recurring GS-I and GS-III themes, and the Kutch recovery is a standard case study for disaster risk reduction and owner-driven rebuilding.

perspectives.take: Carries the IMD's operational forecast of a 'very severe' storm and a 20 November Andhra landfall, and in a separate piece revisits Kutch's 25-year reconstruction record as a governance lesson.

static.topic: Tropical Cyclones in the Bay of Bengal
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Physical Geography of India (Indian Monsoon & Cyclones)
static.whatIsIt: Tropical cyclones are warm-core low-pressure systems that form over warm ocean waters, drawing energy from latent heat released by condensation; in the North Indian Ocean the IMD classifies them from depression to super cyclone according to wind speed.
static.background: Cyclogenesis in the Bay of Bengal peaks in the pre-monsoon (April–May) and post-monsoon (October–December) windows, when sea surface temperatures are high and the ITCZ shifts. The Bay's warm, relatively shallow waters and funnel-shaped coastline make it one of the world's most cyclone-prone basins; the Arabian Sea is comparatively calmer but has recorded more intense systems in recent years.
static.geography: Bay of Bengal coast — Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu; coastal plains and the Eastern Ghats shape storm surge and rainfall distribution.
static.socioEconomic: Cyclones cause loss of life, crop damage, coastal erosion and displacement; fishing communities are among the most exposed, which is why sea advisories precede landfall.
static.whyInNews: IMD has forecast that Cyclone Akvan will intensify into a 'very severe' cyclonic storm and approach the Andhra Pradesh coast around 20 November, the third cyclone threat to the state in three weeks.
static.wayForward: Strengthen multi-hazard early warning, cyclone shelters and last-mile dissemination, and integrate climate projections into coastal land-use planning.
prelimsPointers: IMD classifies a 'very severe cyclonic storm' at wind speeds of 118–166 kmph.
The Bay of Bengal records a far higher frequency of cyclones than the Arabian Sea.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why the Bay of Bengal is a cyclone hotspot and assess the adequacy of India's preparedness along the east coast.

static.topic: Disaster Management Framework in India
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — Institutional Framework
static.whatIsIt: India's disaster management architecture rests on the Disaster Management Act, 2005, which created the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) chaired by the Prime Minister, State and District Disaster Management Authorities, and the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF).
static.background: The Act followed a decade of major disasters, including the 1999 Odisha super cyclone and the 2001 Gujarat (Kutch/Bhuj) earthquake, which exposed gaps in preparedness and reconstruction. The National Policy on Disaster Management (2009) and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030) shifted emphasis from relief towards risk reduction and resilience.
static.socioEconomic: Reconstruction after the 2001 earthquake in Kutch involved a state-level disaster management authority and owner-driven rebuilding, and is often cited as a template for post-disaster recovery.
static.whyInNews: Twenty-five years after the Kutch earthquake, its reconstruction experience is being revisited as a lesson in crisis management, even as a fresh cyclone threat builds over the Bay of Bengal.
static.wayForward: Move from relief-centric response to risk-informed planning; strengthen local capacity, enforcement of building codes and disaster-resilient infrastructure.
prelimsPointers: NDMA is chaired by the Prime Minister; the Disaster Management Act was enacted in 2005.
The Kutch (Bhuj) earthquake struck on 26 January 2001.
static.mainsAngle: Has India's disaster management shifted adequately from relief to risk reduction? Discuss with reference to post-2001 Kutch reconstruction.

static.topic: Disaster Response and Centre-State Coordination
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: Disaster management is not a separately enumerated subject in the Seventh Schedule; response is primarily handled by States, with the Union providing coordination, funding and specialised forces such as the NDRF.
static.background: The Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined Centre-State balance more broadly. In disaster governance, the DM Act 2005 created parallel national and state authorities, and the NDRF is deployed on a State's request.
static.socioEconomic: Funding flows through the State Disaster Response Fund and the National Disaster Response Fund, with Finance Commission norms guiding allocations.
static.whyInNews: As Andhra Pradesh braces for a third cyclone in three weeks, coordination between the IMD, state authorities and central agencies again comes into focus.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise cooperative federalism in disaster governance through joint planning, shared data and predictable financing.
prelimsPointers: The NDRF is a specialised response force under the NDMA, raised in 2006.
The Inter-State Council (Article 263) is a recommendatory body for Centre-State coordination.
static.mainsAngle: Assess how cooperative federalism shapes India's disaster response, using recent cyclone events as examples.

prelims: IMD's cyclone intensity scale runs from depression to super cyclone; a 'very severe cyclonic storm' has wind speeds of 118–166 kmph.
The Bay of Bengal generates a much larger share of India's cyclones than the Arabian Sea, with peaks in the pre-monsoon and post-monsoon months.

stories.mainsQuestion: Cyclones recur almost annually on India's east coast, yet their human and economic impact varies with preparedness. Discuss how post-disaster reconstruction experience — such as Kutch after the 2001 earthquake — can inform India's disaster risk reduction framework.

stories.headline: RBI reiterates Tata Sons listing demand amid family feud
stories.summary: The RBI has reiterated that Tata Sons must comply with its upper-layer NBFC listing requirement, leaving the Tata group holding company with little regulatory room to avoid a public listing. The demand has become entangled in a family dispute: Jimmy N Tata has backed the listing, saying it would dismantle a culture of secrecy, while accusing his half-brother Noel Tata of a 'back-door takeover' by packing the Tata Trusts with family members. Reports profile Jimmy Tata as a reclusive brother of Ratan Tata who is now at odds with Noel Tata. The RBI's stance is significant because Tata Sons is a core investment company/NBFC, and listing would bring greater disclosure and governance scrutiny.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests RBI's regulatory resolve over a major NBFC and the intersection of corporate governance, family control, and public disclosure in India's largest conglomerate.

static.topic: RBI as central bank and financial regulator
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Monetary Policy; Financial Sector Regulation
static.whatIsIt: India's central bank, established in 1935 (nationalised 1949) under the RBI Act, 1934. It conducts monetary policy through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), instituted in 2016 with an inflation-targeting mandate of 4% CPI (±2%). It also regulates banks and NBFCs, manages forex reserves, and acts as banker to government.
static.background: The MPC framework came from the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and a 2016 RBI Act amendment. Tools: repo/reverse repo, Marginal Standing Facility, Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR), and Open Market Operations.
static.socioEconomic: RBI regulation affects credit allocation, financial stability, and corporate governance through disclosure norms for large NBFCs.
static.whyInNews: RBI has reiterated that Tata Sons, as an upper-layer NBFC, must list on stock exchanges, intensifying a governance dispute within the Tata group.
static.wayForward: Ensure regulatory consistency while balancing market stability; strengthen disclosure norms for large NBFCs and core investment companies.
prelimsPointers: Repo = rate at which RBI lends to banks against securities; reverse repo is the absorbing rate.
MPC has 6 members: 3 RBI (incl. Governor as chair) + 3 external; Governor has casting vote.
Inflation target: 4% CPI, band 2–6%, reviewed every 5 years.
static.mainsAngle: Balance growth support with price stability; examine transmission of rate cuts to borrowers (MCLR/EBLR) and the role of fiscal-monetary coordination.

static.topic: Corporate Governance and Public Listing of NBFCs
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Financial Sector; Corporate Governance
static.whatIsIt: Public listing requires a company to disclose financials, related-party transactions, board composition, and risk factors under SEBI regulations, increasing transparency and accountability.
static.background: In India, listed companies are governed by the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015. RBI's upper-layer NBFC framework requires certain large non-bank lenders to list to enhance market discipline.
static.socioEconomic: Listing can dilute family control, invite public scrutiny, and alter succession and trust structures in family-owned conglomerates.
static.whyInNews: Tata Sons' possible listing under RBI norms has become a flashpoint in the Tata family dispute, with Jimmy Tata backing it as a check on secrecy.
static.wayForward: Strengthen independent oversight, clarify RBI's upper-layer NBFC compliance timelines, and ensure fair treatment of minority and public shareholders.

stories.headline: Supreme Court orders encroachment-free Yamuna floodplain, penalties on states
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has directed that the Yamuna floodplain be kept free of encroachments and has ordered penalties on states that fail to check pollution of the river, framing the issue as a failure of executive enforcement rather than of law. The order comes amid recurring episodes of toxic foam on the Yamuna's Delhi stretch and persistent violations of water-quality norms along a river that passes through several states. Reporting on the ground argues that large sums spent on cosmetic measures such as foam removal have not improved the river's health, and questions claims of political will by 'double engine' governments. Together, the two accounts point to a widening gap between judicial directions, public spending and measurable outcomes in river rejuvenation.
stories.whyItMatters: The order is a live test of judicial enforcement of environmental rights under Article 21 and of Centre–State coordination on a subject where water is a State subject but pollution control is shared. It is directly usable in GS-II (judiciary, federalism) and GS-III (environment, pollution, governance) answers.

perspectives.take: Legal-institutional framing: highlights the Court's directions on clearing floodplain encroachments, imposing penalties on defaulting states and fixing accountability on authorities — a judicial-review lens on executive failure.

Ground-level, critical framing in Hindi: lakhs spent on removing foam have left the Yamuna unchanged, and it questions the 'double engine' governance claim — emphasising the spending-versus-outcome gap over the courtroom order.

static.topic: Supreme Court directions on river pollution and judicial enforcement of environmental rights
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Judicial Review, PIL and Enforcement of Fundamental Rights
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution, with writ jurisdiction under Article 32; High Courts exercise parallel power under Article 214 and Article 226. Judicial review allows courts to test executive action and law against the Constitution, and PIL has been the main route for environmental enforcement.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s, and environmental litigation used tools such as continuing mandamus, the polluter-pays and precautionary principles, and the public trust doctrine. Article 142 gives the Court power to pass any order necessary for complete justice.
static.socioEconomic: River pollution disproportionately burdens downstream urban poor households dependent on the river for water, fishing and informal livelihoods, while clean-up costs are borne publicly.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court has ordered an encroachment-free Yamuna floodplain and directed penalties on states failing to control pollution, continuing a long line of judicial interventions on the river.
static.wayForward: Convert episodic judicial directions into time-bound, audited compliance frameworks with named nodal officers, published water-quality data and independent verification, so that enforcement does not depend on repeated court orders.
prelimsPointers: Article 21 has been interpreted to include the right to a clean and healthy environment; Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty) also cover environmental protection.
Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court lies in disputes between the Centre and states under Article 131; advisory jurisdiction is under Article 143.
The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 created a specialised forum for environmental disputes.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether judicially driven environmental enforcement can substitute for executive capacity, and assess the balance between judicial activism and institutional restraint.

static.topic: Centre–State coordination in controlling pollution of an inter-state river
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution: Centre–State Relations and the Seventh Schedule
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union: powers are divided by the Union, State and Concurrent Lists in the Seventh Schedule, with residuary powers with the Union under Article 248. Water is a State subject, while pollution control operates through concurrent and consensual legislative routes, making inter-state rivers a shared responsibility.
static.background: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) examined Centre–State balance. Because water is a State subject, the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was enacted by Parliament under Article 252 after resolutions by states; the CPCB and State Pollution Control Boards were constituted under it. Article 254 governs repugnancy on Concurrent List subjects, and Article 263 provides for an Inter-State Council.
static.geography: The Yamuna rises in Uttarakhand and flows through Haryana, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh before joining the Ganga at Prayagraj, so its pollution load and floodplain management cut across multiple state jurisdictions.
static.socioEconomic: Urban sewage, industrial effluent and encroached floodplains impose health costs and flood risk on downstream cities, while clean-up is funded from public budgets across several states.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court's direction to penalise states over Yamuna pollution sharpens the question of how the Union, states and municipal bodies share responsibility for an inter-state river.
static.wayForward: Strengthen river-basin level institutions with statutory backing, link central funds to verified water-quality outcomes, and use the Inter-State Council for binding coordination rather than advisory consultation alone.
prelimsPointers: Water is a State subject (Entry 17, List II); the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was enacted under Article 252 after states passed enabling resolutions.
Under Article 254, on a Concurrent List subject the Union law prevails on repugnancy unless the state law has been reserved for and received the President's assent.
The Inter-State Council under Article 263 is a recommendatory body for coordination and dispute resolution.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether India's federal design and municipal capacity are adequate to clean inter-state rivers, and suggest institutional reforms for enforceable basin-level accountability.

static.topic: Floodplains, monsoon flows and river health
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Physical Geography of India: Drainage Systems and the Monsoon
static.whatIsIt: Floodplains act as natural sponges that absorb peak monsoon discharge and recharge groundwater. The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by differential heating, the ITCZ shift and the Tibetan Plateau's heat pump, delivering about 75% of annual rainfall during June–September.
static.background: El Niño usually weakens the monsoon, La Niña strengthens it, and the Indian Ocean Dipole modulates it. Himalayan rivers such as the Yamuna are perennial and snow-fed, while peninsular rivers are rain-fed and seasonal; encroachment on floodplains removes the buffer that absorbs high flows.
static.geography: The Yamuna is the longest tributary of the Ganga, rising from the Yamunotri glacier in Uttarakhand and joining the Ganga at Prayagraj; its floodplain in the Delhi region is heavily built over.
static.socioEconomic: Encroached floodplains raise urban flood risk and displace informal settlements during high-flow months, while also reducing groundwater recharge for surrounding areas.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court's insistence on an encroachment-free Yamuna floodplain links river pollution to the loss of the floodplain's hydrological function.
static.wayForward: Notify and enforce floodplain zoning regulations, protect e-flows, and integrate floodplain restoration with urban drainage and sewage treatment planning.
prelimsPointers: Himalayan rivers are perennial and snow-fed; peninsular rivers are rain-fed and seasonal.
The Yamuna is the longest tributary of the Ganga, originating from the Yamunotri glacier and meeting the Ganga at Prayagraj.
About 75% of India's annual rainfall is received during the June–September monsoon.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how floodplain encroachment and monsoon variability interact to increase urban flood risk, and evaluate floodplain zoning as a mitigation tool.

prelims: The Yamuna rises from the Yamunotri glacier in Uttarakhand and joins the Ganga at Prayagraj; it is the longest tributary of the Ganga.
Article 21 has been read to include the right to a clean environment, supported by Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty).
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was enacted under Article 252 because water is a State subject; it created the CPCB and State Pollution Control Boards.
The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 established a specialised adjudicatory body for environmental matters.
stories.mainsQuestion: Judicial directions and large public expenditures have not restored the Yamuna's health. Examine why court-driven enforcement has been insufficient, and suggest an institutional framework combining federal coordination, municipal capacity and enforceable accountability for river rejuvenation.

stories.headline: US sends third carrier to West Asia; Saudi replaces Yemen commander
stories.summary: A third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, has arrived in West Asia, an unusually high concentration of American carrier power that Washington is presenting as keeping options open in its conflict with Iran. In parallel, Saudi Arabia has replaced its military commander for Yemen after Houthi forces made rapid gains against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, with the renewed US–Iran confrontation having re-ignited Yemen's frozen civil war and drawn Riyadh back into direct confrontation with the group. The wider region remains unsettled: an analysis warns that drone warfare in Sudan has erased rear-area safety, hitting markets, hospitals, transport hubs and homes, while in Israel opposition leaders accused Prime Minister Netanyahu of an 'attempted coup' after he alleged electoral fraud by Arab parties that had won a record number of seats. Together the developments point to a West Asia–Red Sea–Horn of Africa arc in which external military deployments, proxy conflicts and domestic political contestation are increasingly interlinked.
stories.whyItMatters: West Asia is a recurring UPSC theme under GS-II International Relations — India's energy security, diaspora safety, chokepoint stability (Bab-el-Mandeb, Strait of Hormuz) and its balancing act between the US, Gulf states, Israel and Iran all hinge on these dynamics. The drone-warfare and command-shake-up angles also feed GS-III internal security and GS-I geography questions on conflict spillover.

perspectives.take: Bundles the third US carrier deployment, the Saudi command change, Sudan's drone-war analysis and Israel's political crisis into one connected regional-escalation frame, stressing spillover rather than isolated events.
Wire-service, event-first framing: leads narrowly on the Yemen setback and the replacement of the Saudi military commander, with minimal wider regional context or interpretation.

static.topic: US military posture in West Asia and the Iran confrontation
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: The stationing of US naval and air assets, including aircraft carrier strike groups, in West Asia as a signalling and deterrence instrument. A carrier strike group typically comprises the carrier plus escorting cruisers, destroyers and supply ships, and its presence is read as a political signal as much as a military one.
static.background: The US has maintained a continuous naval presence in the Gulf and Arabian Sea since the 1990s, reinforced during the 1991 Gulf War, the 2003 Iraq invasion and the campaign against the Islamic State. Carrier deployments have repeatedly been surged during periods of tension with Iran, including after the 2018 US withdrawal from the JCPOA and subsequent regional flare-ups. The current build-up follows the renewed US–Iran conflict.
static.geography: West Asia littoral — Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, Gulf of Oman, Arabian Sea and the Red Sea/Bab-el-Mandeb chokepoint, through which a large share of India's crude and LNG imports and much of India–Europe trade passes.
static.socioEconomic: Escalation raises freight and insurance costs, crude price volatility and remittance risk for India's large Gulf diaspora; Indian exports to the region and shipping through the Red Sea are directly exposed.
static.whyInNews: A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in West Asia, an unusually high number, as Washington keeps options open in its conflict with Iran.
static.wayForward: India should deepen contingency planning for energy supply diversification, evacuation of diaspora (Operation-type contingency protocols) and continued diplomatic outreach to both Gulf capitals and Tehran to preserve its strategic autonomy.
prelimsPointers: Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and is the world's most critical oil chokepoint.
Bab-el-Mandeb links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and lies off Yemen, Djibouti and Eritrea.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how great-power military deployments in West Asia affect India's energy security, diaspora safety and strategic autonomy, and suggest a calibrated Indian response.

static.topic: Yemen civil war and the Houthi insurgency
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global groupings and their impact on India; neighbourhood and extended neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: A multi-sided civil war in Yemen pitting the Iran-aligned Houthi movement against the internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by a Saudi-led coalition, alongside southern separatist and local armed groups.
static.background: The Houthis took control of Yemen's capital Sana'a in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition intervention in 2015. A UN-brokered nationwide truce in 2022 substantially reduced fighting but lapsed without a permanent settlement, leaving a 'frozen' conflict that has repeatedly re-ignited. The Houthis have also launched attacks on Red Sea shipping, disrupting global trade routes.
static.geography: Yemen sits at the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, commanding Bab-el-Mandeb and the southern Red Sea — a chokepoint for Suez-bound traffic.
static.socioEconomic: Yemen has long been described by the UN as facing one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with mass displacement, food insecurity and collapsed public services; renewed fighting worsens access and aid delivery.
static.whyInNews: Houthi forces have made rapid gains against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since the US–Iran conflict re-ignited Yemen's frozen civil war, prompting Saudi Arabia to replace its military commander.
static.wayForward: A durable settlement requires a Yemeni-owned political process under UN auspices, credible security guarantees for the Red Sea corridor, and de-escalation between Riyadh and Tehran so that Yemen is not used as a proxy arena.
prelimsPointers: Yemen's capital is Sana'a; Aden is its principal southern port city.
Yemen borders Saudi Arabia to the north and Oman to the east, and faces Djibouti and Eritrea across Bab-el-Mandeb.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the Yemen conflict illustrates the intersection of proxy rivalry, chokepoint security and humanitarian crisis, and evaluate the prospects for a UN-led political settlement.

static.topic: Drone warfare and the erosion of safe zones in armed conflict
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Role of external state and non-state actors; Security challenges and their management
static.whatIsIt: The use of unmanned aerial systems — from loitering munitions to weaponised quadcopters — to strike targets, disrupt logistics and extend the battlefield deep into previously secure rear areas.
static.background: Drone use expanded from state counter-terrorism operations to full-scale inter-state and civil wars, notably in Nagorno-Karabakh, Ukraine, and now Sudan. Falling costs, commercial component availability and improved targeting have democratised precision strike capability for both state forces and non-state groups.
static.geography: Sudan — Africa's third-largest country by area, spanning the Sahel and the Red Sea coast, bordering Egypt, Libya, Chad, the Central African Republic, South Sudan, Ethiopia and Eritrea.
static.socioEconomic: Strikes on markets, hospitals and transport hubs deepen humanitarian crisis, displace populations, disrupt supply chains and complicate aid delivery; Sudan's conflict has already produced large-scale displacement and food insecurity.
static.whyInNews: An analysis notes that drone strikes in Sudan are disrupting supply lines and expanding the battlefield into previously secure areas, targeting markets, hospitals, transport hubs and homes and heightening civilian risk.
static.wayForward: Strengthening compliance with international humanitarian law — distinction, proportionality and precaution — plus export controls on drone components, counter-UAS capabilities and accountability mechanisms for unlawful strikes.
prelimsPointers: Sudan's capital is Khartoum; the country has a Red Sea coastline and the Nile confluence at Khartoum.
IHL core principles: distinction, proportionality, precaution and military necessity.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse how the proliferation of drone technology is transforming the character of armed conflict and what it implies for civilian protection, IHL compliance and India's internal security preparedness.

prelims: A third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, has arrived in West Asia — an unusually high concentration of American carrier strength in the region.
Saudi Arabia has replaced its military commander for Yemen after rapid Houthi gains against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
The renewed US–Iran confrontation is credited with re-igniting Yemen's previously frozen civil war, drawing Riyadh back into confrontation with the Houthis.
Drone strikes in Sudan are now hitting markets, hospitals, transport hubs and homes, erasing the distinction between front line and safe rear areas.
stories.mainsQuestion: The re-ignition of the Yemen conflict alongside a fresh US–Iran confrontation shows how West Asian flashpoints are increasingly interlinked. Examine the implications for India's energy security, diaspora safety and strategic autonomy, and suggest an appropriate diplomatic and contingency response.

stories.headline: Six Liangmai Naga civilians buried in Manipur 187 days after killing; strike rocks Imphal
stories.summary: The bodies of six Liangmai Naga civilians were interred in Manipur, 187 days after they were abducted and killed, closing a long wait for the families even as questions over accountability remain unanswered. The United Naga Council president, N.G. Lorho, described May 13, 2026, as the darkest day in the State's history, framing the episode as a failure of protection for hill communities. Simultaneously, a statewide strike called over the killing of Naga civilians brought Imphal to a halt, with police firing tear gas shells to disperse protesters. Accounts differ on the toll, with some reports referring to four Naga civilians killed, indicating the difficulty of verifying ground details amid restricted access and curfews. The events underline the persistence of ethnic polarisation in Manipur and the strain on the State's law-and-order and grievance-redress machinery.
stories.whyItMatters: Ethnic violence and delayed justice in Manipur test India's internal-security framework, the credibility of state institutions, and Centre-State coordination in the Northeast — a recurring theme for GS-II governance and GS-III internal security questions.

perspectives.take: Frames the story around grief, delay and impunity — centring the 187-day wait for burial and the UNC president's description of May 13, 2026, as Manipur's darkest day.
Frames it as a law-and-order crisis — statewide strike, tear gas in Imphal and disruption, with a lower reported toll of four civilians, reflecting a security/dispatch lens.

static.topic: Federalism and Centre-State Relations in Conflict Zones
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union: powers are divided between the Union and States via the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule), with residuary powers with the Union (Article 248). In states under internal disturbance, the Union's constitutional and administrative role expands sharply through the Governor, central forces and Article 355 duties.
static.background: Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions examined the Centre-State balance. The Governor (Article 153) is the Centre's constitutional representative and a recurring flashpoint over assent to Bills (Article 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Article 201). In the Northeast, statehood was progressively granted — Nagaland (1963), Meghalaya (1972), Manipur and Tripura (1972) — with special provisions and ongoing peace processes shaping the Union's role.
static.geography: Manipur is a landlocked hill-and-valley state bordering Myanmar, with the Imphal Valley dominated by Meiteis and the surrounding hills inhabited largely by Naga and Kuki-Zo communities — a demographic geography central to the conflict.
static.socioEconomic: Hill districts lag in connectivity, employment and public services; competition over land, tribal status claims and administrative boundaries feeds ethnic mobilisation, while blockades and strikes disrupt supplies to the valley.
static.whyInNews: Six Liangmai Naga civilians were buried 187 days after their abduction and killing, and a statewide strike over the deaths triggered tear gas firing by police in Imphal.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise independent, time-bound probes into civilian killings, strengthen district-level grievance redress and tribal consultation mechanisms, and use the Inter-State Council and North Eastern Council for coordinated confidence-building rather than reactive deployment.
prelimsPointers: Concurrent List: union law prevails on repugnancy unless the state law is reserved for and receives the President's assent (Article 254).
Inter-State Council (Article 263) is a recommendatory body for inquiry into and advice on inter-state disputes.
static.mainsAngle: Ethnic conflict in a state raises questions of federal responsibility and accountability — examine whether existing Centre-State mechanisms are adequate to protect minority communities and deliver timely justice.

static.topic: Ethnic Conflict and Internal Security in the Northeast
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Role of Non-State Actors, Extremism and Ethnic Violence
static.whatIsIt: Manipur has witnessed sustained ethnic confrontation between Meitei and Kuki-Zo/Naga groups since 2023, marked by blockades, arson, civilian killings and prolonged internet shutdowns, with security forces stretched between containment and relief duties.
static.background: The Northeast has seen decades of insurgent movements and successive peace accords with Naga and other groups. The United Naga Council, an apex body of Naga tribes in Manipur, has historically mobilised on identity, territorial and administrative demands. AFSPA (1958) continues to apply to parts of the region, and its phased withdrawal has been a long-standing demand.
static.geography: Manipur shares a porous border with Myanmar, facilitating arms and narcotics flows and complicating security operations; hill-valley terrain constrains mobility for both administration and relief.
static.socioEconomic: Displacement, loss of livelihoods, closure of markets and disruption of the National Highways have deepened economic distress; strikes and blockades amplify supply shortages and price spikes.
static.whyInNews: A statewide strike over the killing of Naga civilians led to tear gas firing in Imphal, alongside the burial of six abducted and killed Liangmai Naga men.
static.wayForward: Prioritise credible investigations and prosecutions in civilian killings, restore and monitor arterial highway access, pursue inclusive political dialogue involving all communities and civil society, and sequence AFSPA review with demonstrable improvements in local policing.
prelimsPointers: The Liangmai are a Naga tribe; the Rongmei, Zeme and Liangmai together are often described as the Zeliangrong group.
The United Naga Council is an apex body representing Naga tribes in Manipur's hill districts.
static.mainsAngle: Ethnic violence in Manipur persists despite deployment of central forces — analyse the limitations of a purely security-centric response and suggest a governance-led approach.

prelims: Liangmai is a Naga tribe; with the Rongmei and Zeme, it is grouped under the Zeliangrong identity in the Northeast.
The United Naga Council is an apex organisation of Naga tribes in Manipur; its president is N.G. Lorho.
AFSPA (Armed Forces Special Powers Act) dates to 1958 and remains in force in parts of the Northeast, including sections of Manipur.
Manipur attained statehood in 1972, alongside Tripura and Meghalaya, under the North Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) framework.
stories.mainsQuestion: Ethnic violence in Manipur has repeatedly exposed the gap between security deployment and justice delivery. Examine the causes of persistent Naga-Meitei-Kuki friction and suggest a governance-led framework for durable peace in the state.

stories.headline: Trump backs Jensen Huang's Nvidia return as board rules it out
stories.summary: Reports from CNBC and Reuters say Nvidia's board is not considering bringing founder Jensen Huang back as CEO, even as a campaign for his return gathers support among investors and the company prepares its first briefing on life after Huang. US President Donald Trump said he would 'certainly not mind' a reinstatement, remarked that Huang had 'learned a big lesson', and dismissed spy allegations involving a Chinese woman connected to the affair. The Hindu BusinessLine reports that the board's refusal has divided investors and sharpened scrutiny of Nvidia's succession planning. Running alongside the boardroom drama, an Indian Express explainer asks whether China trained its most advanced AI models on Nvidia chips that US export rules bar it from buying, and the same paper reports that Trump's own Nvidia holdings rose nearly 100-fold during the row.
stories.whyItMatters: The episode bundles three exam-relevant threads: the extreme concentration of the global AI chip supply chain, the use of export controls as strategic leverage in the US–China contest, and the test of board independence in CEO succession at a systemically important firm.

perspectives.take: Business-news framing: the board's refusal to restore Huang deepens succession uncertainty and has split the investor base.
Wire-service framing: Nvidia is preparing its first 'life-after-Huang' briefing and has ruled out a comeback even as the return campaign grows.
Politically angled coverage of Trump's personal endorsement, the spy-allegation spectacle, and the reported surge in his own Nvidia holdings.
International-desk focus on Trump's remark that he 'would not mind' a reinstatement, noting a 'big group' of people wants Huang back.
Short-format panel framing the story as Silicon Valley versus Washington, with an Indian-audience geopolitical lens.

Sourcing-first business report: a source close to the matter says the board is not considering bringing Huang back.
Analytical framing: with the board opposed, few institutional pathways remain for a Huang return.

static.topic: India Semiconductor Mission and the global chip supply chain
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Industrial Policy; Science & Technology — Emerging Technologies
static.whatIsIt: A ₹76,000-crore programme under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), launched in December 2021 under the Semicon India Programme, to build domestic fabrication (fabs), display fabs, compound-semiconductor/ATMP-OSAT units and chip design capacity through the Design Linked Incentive scheme.
static.background: India's earlier fab attempts (including the 2007 SemIndia proposal) failed. Under the India Semiconductor Mission the Union Cabinet approved, in 2024, India's first proposed commercial fab at Dholera, Gujarat (Tata Electronics with Taiwan's Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp) and assembly-test-packaging units at Jagiroad (Assam) and Sanand (Gujarat), among others. Semiconductor supply-chain cooperation is a pillar of the India–US initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET, 2023).
static.geography: Dholera and Sanand in Gujarat (fab and ATMP); Jagiroad, Morigaon district, Assam (OSAT); design clusters in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Noida.
static.socioEconomic: Chips underpin telecom, automobiles, defence and AI, making import dependence a strategic vulnerability. Fab and OSAT clusters create skilled jobs but need large capital, water, power and a trained workforce.
static.whyInNews: The Nvidia boardroom turmoil and the US–China export-control debate spotlight how concentrated the AI chip supply chain is, and why India is pushing fab and packaging capacity.
static.wayForward: Move from assembly toward fabrication and design; secure equipment, materials and critical minerals; deepen iCET-type partnerships and expand the semiconductor-skilling pipeline.
prelimsPointers: ISM outlay is ₹76,000 crore; the nodal ministry is MeitY.
India's first proposed commercial fab is at Dholera, Gujarat, targeting mature nodes rather than leading-edge logic.
Leading-edge logic manufacturing remains concentrated in TSMC (Taiwan), Samsung (South Korea) and Intel (US).
static.mainsAngle: How far can India's semiconductor mission reduce strategic import dependence? Discuss with reference to the global division of labour in chip-making.

static.topic: US export controls on advanced semiconductors and China's AI question
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies of developed countries on India's interests; technology and strategic controls
static.whatIsIt: Successive US restrictions, administered by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) in the US Department of Commerce, on exports to China of advanced computing chips, semiconductor manufacturing equipment and high-bandwidth memory, enforced through the Entity List and the Foreign Direct Product Rule.
static.background: Sweeping controls began in October 2022 (covering Nvidia's A100 and H100), were tightened in October 2023 and again in December 2024, when high-bandwidth memory and additional tool categories were added. Nvidia responded with China-specific, lower-spec chips such as the H20. The January 2025 'AI diffusion rule' was rescinded in May 2025. China retaliated with export curbs on gallium, germanium and graphite, and later on rare earths.
static.geography: Chokepoints include Taiwan (TSMC manufacturing), the Netherlands (ASML's EUV lithography), Japan (materials and equipment), South Korea (memory) and China (assembly and rare-earth refining).
static.socioEconomic: Controls raise costs and fragment supply chains, pushing China toward indigenous substitutes and prompting 'friend-shoring' of capacity to India, Vietnam and Mexico.
static.whyInNews: An explainer examines whether China trained its most advanced AI models on Nvidia chips that US rules bar it from importing, even as the Nvidia leadership row plays out.
static.wayForward: India should use strategic autonomy to secure long-term supply and technology arrangements, and pair market access with indigenous design and fabrication capacity rather than remaining a swing market.
prelimsPointers: US chip export controls are administered by BIS under the US Department of Commerce.
EUV lithography machines, essential for leading-edge chips, are supplied only by ASML of the Netherlands.
Nvidia is a fabless designer; it does not own fabs and depends on TSMC for manufacturing.
static.mainsAngle: Do unilateral export controls on advanced technology serve their strategic purpose, or do they accelerate indigenous substitution? Discuss with reference to the US–China chip contest.

static.topic: Corporate governance, board independence and CEO succession
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Corporate Governance and Capital Markets
static.whatIsIt: The framework of board independence, disclosure and shareholder protection governing how large listed companies select, evaluate and remove top management; in India it flows from the Companies Act, 2013 and the SEBI (LODR) Regulations.
static.background: India's modern governance framework traces to the Kumar Mangalam Birla Committee (1999), the Naresh Chandra Committee (2002) and the Narayana Murthy Committee (2003), followed by the Companies Act, 2013 (independent directors, audit committees, related-party disclosures) and SEBI's LODR Regulations, 2015. In the US, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, 2002 followed the Enron and WorldCom collapses.
static.socioEconomic: Founder-CEO dominance in technology firms concentrates power and raises succession risk; perceived governance quality directly affects investor confidence and valuations.
static.whyInNews: Nvidia's board has ruled out the return of founder-CEO Jensen Huang even as political and investor pressure builds — a live test of board independence and succession planning.
static.wayForward: Strengthen genuine board independence, mandate disclosure of succession plans and separate the chair and CEO roles in the largest listed entities.
prelimsPointers: The Companies Act, 2013 mandates independent directors and audit committees for prescribed classes of companies.
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act, 2002 was the US legislative response to the Enron and WorldCom accounting scandals.
static.mainsAngle: Board independence is often asserted but rarely tested. Examine the role of independent directors in CEO succession and accountability in large listed companies.

prelims: Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO, according to sources cited by CNBC and Reuters.
US President Donald Trump said he would 'not mind' Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia, adding that Huang had 'learned a big lesson'.
The leadership row runs parallel to a debate over whether China trained its most advanced AI models on Nvidia chips banned from export to it.
US curbs on advanced chip exports to China are administered by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), US Department of Commerce.
stories.mainsQuestion: The semiconductor supply chain has become a theatre of geopolitical contest. Examine how US export controls on advanced chips shape China's AI ambitions and India's semiconductor strategy, and assess the governance questions raised by leadership succession at firms of systemic importance.

stories.headline: UP poll prep, Bengal feuds test BJP; Congress-SP seat talks advance
stories.summary: With Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections approaching, the BJP held a key Mathura meeting to discuss organisational programmes, booth empowerment, welfare delivery, caste outreach and poll strategy, even as TheWire reported internal disquiet over a 209-candidate manoeuvre. The Congress leadership signalled it is negotiating a seat-sharing deal with the Samajwadi Party and is eyeing more than 100 seats. In West Bengal, a Union minister alleged that BJP supporters were attacking fellow party members, and the killing of a BJP worker—allegedly by party members—triggered calls from the ranks to stop inducting former TMC workers. A Murshidabad BJP leader's proposed social rulebook and questions over the roles of Maneka and Varun Gandhi added to the picture of internal churn across the party.
stories.whyItMatters: UP is India's largest state by Assembly seats and a national bellwether; alliance arithmetic and party cohesion can shape broader political trajectories. Internal party management also affects candidate selection, representation and electoral credibility.

perspectives.take: Reports the Mathura meeting as a strategy and organisational reset, while its Bengal reports foreground a minister's allegation of intra-party violence and a worker's murder.
Focuses on Congress-SP seat-sharing pragmatics and, from Bengal, rank-and-file demand to curb TMC inductions after a worker's death.

static.topic: Indian National Congress and coalition politics
static.syllabusNode: Modern Indian History — National Movement and Party Evolution
static.whatIsIt: The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, led the national movement and later became a central actor in India's party system and coalition politics.
static.background: Founded by A.O. Hume in 1885; key milestones include the Swadeshi movement after the 1905 Partition of Bengal, Non-Cooperation (1920), Civil Disobedience and Dandi March (1930), Quit India (1942), and the 1947 Indian Independence Act.
static.socioEconomic: Its historical mass base and social coalition inform its contemporary alliance strategies, including seat-sharing with regional parties.
static.whyInNews: Congress is negotiating a UP poll deal with the Samajwadi Party and is eyeing over 100 seats.
static.wayForward: Assess how a historical mass party adapts its coalition and organisational strategies in a competitive multi-party era.

static.topic: Welfare delivery and electoral outreach
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare Architecture and Rights
static.whatIsIt: India's welfare model combines rights-based laws such as MGNREGA, RTE and NFSA with DBT and the JAM delivery backbone.
static.background: Ayushman Bharat (2018) includes PM-JAY and Health & Wellness Centres; POSHAN Abhiyaan targets malnutrition; Articles 15/16 and Indra Sawhney (1992) frame reservation policy.
static.socioEconomic: Welfare benefits and caste-based outreach are used in electoral mobilisation, especially in large states such as Uttar Pradesh.
static.whyInNews: The BJP's Mathura meeting discussed public welfare benefits and caste-based outreach ahead of Assembly polls.
static.wayForward: Strengthen last-mile delivery and evaluate whether welfare expansion improves capability or entrenches patronage.

static.mainsAngle: Examine the use of welfare schemes as electoral instruments and its implications for democratic accountability.

static.topic: Election Commission and electoral conduct
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Elections and Electoral Machinery
static.whatIsIt: The Election Commission of India, a constitutional body under Article 324, superintends elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President.
static.background: Established on 25 January 1950; it became a multi-member body in 1993; the Model Code of Conduct evolved through political consensus and ECI enforcement.
static.socioEconomic: UP, India's most populous state, has a 403-seat Assembly and sends 80 members to the Lok Sabha, making its polls nationally significant.
static.whyInNews: UP Assembly poll preparations and Congress-SP seat-sharing talks have begun.
static.wayForward: Ensure a level playing field through transparent candidate disclosure and robust MCC enforcement.
prelimsPointers: The ECI was established on 25 January 1950 under Article 324.
Uttar Pradesh has a 403-seat Legislative Assembly and 80 Lok Sabha seats.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the ECI's role in maintaining electoral integrity amid pre-poll alliances and internal party disputes.

stories.headline: Apex Court, High Courts rule on library, NBT status, NDPS courts
stories.summary: On 16 November 2026, the Supreme Court and several High Courts delivered a cluster of orders spanning institutional autonomy, constitutional definitions and criminal-justice administration. The Supreme Court halted the shifting of the 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library, and separately ruled that the National Book Trust falls within the ambit of 'State' under Article 12, making it amenable to fundamental-rights scrutiny. In the same week the Court observed that the law does not guarantee that any particular constituency will be reserved for SC/STs, and directed the Centre and States to file status reports on the setting up of special courts under the NDPS Act. Among the High Courts, Kerala referred a petition challenging the clean chit to the Chief Minister in the Punarjani case to the Chief Justice for allocation of the appropriate roster, the Allahabad High Court asked the ED to file an affidavit on whether grounds of arrest were served on Azam Khan, and the Bombay High Court warned that using criminal cases to stifle peaceful protest would be a 'sad day for democracy'. Weekly round-ups from the Delhi High Court and the Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court, along with remarks by a Madras High Court judge, rounded off a heavy judicial week.
stories.whyItMatters: The week illustrates the widening canvas of judicial review — from the autonomy of cultural institutions and the meaning of 'State' under Article 12 to the operational capacity of special courts and the procedural safeguards around arrest. These are recurring UPSC themes under Polity (Judiciary, Fundamental Rights) and governance.
