static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts, judicial review, writ jurisdiction and PIL
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power of courts to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution, exercised through writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 (Supreme Court) and 226 (High Courts).
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. Public Interest Litigation expanded access to justice from the late 1970s, allowing the Court to take up matters of institutional and public concern — the mode in which several of this week's orders arose.
static.socioEconomic: Pendency and vacancies in the higher judiciary affect the pace of constitutional adjudication; PIL-driven interventions on institutional autonomy and protest-related prosecutions carry direct implications for civil liberties and public trust in courts.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court stayed the shifting of the 135-year-old Central Secretariat Library, ruled on the National Book Trust's status under Article 12, commented on SC/ST constituency reservation, and sought status reports on NDPS special courts; High Courts in Kerala, Allahabad, Bombay and Madras passed significant orders and observations.
static.wayForward: Strengthen case-flow management and vacancy filling, rationalise roster and PIL allocation through clear registry practice, and ensure that judicial intervention in institutional matters is exercised with reasoned, narrowly tailored orders.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction: disputes between the Centre and States (Article 131).
Advisory jurisdiction under Article 143.
Article 32 provides the right to constitutional remedies before the Supreme Court; Article 226 gives High Courts wider writ jurisdiction.
static.mainsAngle: Examine judicial backlog, vacancies and pendency; the balance between judicial independence and accountability; and the appropriate limits of PIL-based intervention in institutional autonomy.

static.topic: Article 12 'State', Statutory Bodies and Special Courts under the NDPS Act
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process: statutory bodies, delegated implementation and special courts
static.whatIsIt: Article 12 defines 'State' for Part III of the Constitution to include the Government and Parliament of India, State governments and legislatures, local authorities, and 'other authorities' within India or under the control of the Government of India. Statutory bodies such as the National Book Trust may fall within 'other authorities' depending on the degree of state control. The NDPS Act, 1985 provides for the constitution of special courts to try offences under it.
static.background: The scope of 'other authorities' under Article 12 has been expanded through a line of Supreme Court decisions applying tests such as financial control, functional character and deep and pervasive state control. Special courts are a legislative device to speed up trial of offences under statutes such as the NDPS Act, whose cases often involve long pre-trial detention.
static.socioEconomic: Delay in constituting special courts contributes to undertrial overcrowding and prolonged detention in drug-offence cases; bringing bodies like the National Book Trust within Article 12 makes their actions testable against fundamental rights, including Articles 14 and 19.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court ruled on the National Book Trust's status as 'State' under Article 12, and separately directed the Centre and States to file status reports on the setting up of NDPS special courts.
static.wayForward: Notify and operationalise special courts with adequate infrastructure, prosecutors and forensic support; publish periodic compliance data; and ensure statutory bodies maintain transparent, non-arbitrary decision-making consistent with fundamental rights.
prelimsPointers: Article 12 lists the Government and Parliament of India, State governments and legislatures, local authorities, and other authorities as 'State'.
The NDPS Act, 1985 is the principal central law on narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances and provides for special courts.
A writ of mandamus lies to compel a public authority to perform a statutory duty.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the expanding definition of 'State' under Article 12 strengthens accountability of statutory bodies, and evaluate the institutional bottlenecks in operationalising special courts for statutes like the NDPS Act.

static.topic: Reservation of Constituencies for SC/STs and Delimitation
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Representation and Elections: reservation of seats in legislatures and delimitation
static.whatIsIt: Articles 330 and 332 provide for reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and in State Legislative Assemblies respectively, in proportion to their population. Which specific constituencies are reserved is determined through the delimitation exercise, not by a guarantee attaching to any particular seat.
static.background: Delimitation has been carried out by Delimitation Commissions; the 84th Constitutional Amendment (2001) froze the total number of Lok Sabha seats and the inter-State allocation of seats until the first census after 2026, while allowing readjustment of constituency boundaries within States on the basis of the 2001 Census (later modified by the 87th Amendment).
static.geography: Reserved constituencies are distributed across States in proportion to SC/ST population, so the identity of a reserved seat can change after each delimitation exercise.
static.socioEconomic: Reservation of constituencies is intended to ensure legislative representation for SC/ST communities; rotation of reserved seats can affect incumbency patterns and local political dynamics.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court observed that the law does not guarantee that any particular constituency will be reserved for SC/STs.
static.wayForward: Ensure delimitation exercises are transparent, data-driven and completed within constitutionally mandated timelines, with clear public communication on the rotation of reserved constituencies.
prelimsPointers: Article 330 provides for reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha; Article 332 does the same for State Legislative Assemblies.
The 84th Amendment (2001) froze the total number of Lok Sabha seats and inter-State allocation until the first census after 2026.
Reservation of seats is proportionate to population; the specific constituencies reserved are determined by delimitation.
static.mainsAngle: Examine the constitutional scheme of reserved constituencies and the implications of delimitation timelines for representation, federal balance and electoral certainty.

stories.headline: Gujarat to receive water as 30-year inter-state dispute is settled
stories.summary: A water-sharing dispute involving Gujarat that ran for roughly three decades has been brought to a close, with a new inter-state arrangement under which Gujarat is set to receive water. The settlement was reported by The Indian Express, which frames it as the resolution of a long-pending disagreement between states over the sharing of river water. Such disputes are typically handled either through negotiated agreements between the states concerned or through adjudication by a tribunal constituted under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, with Article 262 of the Constitution providing the enabling framework. The operational details of the arrangement — allocation volumes, timelines and monitoring — are expected to determine how durable the settlement proves in practice.
stories.whyItMatters: Inter-state river water disputes sit at the intersection of federalism, constitutional design (Article 262) and resource politics, and are a recurring theme in GS-II polity and GS-I geography questions. Settlements also test whether cooperative federalism can deliver outcomes that tribunals alone often cannot.

static.topic: Inter-State River Water Disputes and Article 262
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: Article 262 empowers Parliament to provide, by law, for the adjudication of disputes relating to the waters of inter-state rivers and river valleys, and to bar the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other courts in such matters. Parliament used this power to enact the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, under which ad hoc tribunals are constituted to adjudicate disputes that states cannot settle by negotiation.
static.background: Water and water supplies are primarily State subjects (Entry 17, State List), while regulation and development of inter-state rivers and river valleys falls in the Union List (Entry 56). The ISRWD Act, 1956 was amended in 2002 to encourage negotiated settlement through a negotiation-and-mediation route before a tribunal is constituted, and to allow a single tribunal to handle multiple disputes. Tribunals have been set up for several basins over the decades, including the Krishna, Godavari, Narmada, Cauvery, Ravi-Beas, Vansadhara, Mahadayi and Mahanadi disputes. The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) both examined Centre-State and inter-State dispute-resolution arrangements, including the Inter-State Council under Article 263.
static.geography: Inter-state river disputes arise from the physical asymmetry of river basins: upstream states control flows while downstream states depend on them, and monsoon variability, storage projects and irrigation expansion sharpen the conflict. Basin-level planning therefore has to reconcile hydrology with state boundaries.
static.socioEconomic: Water allocation directly affects irrigation coverage, farm incomes, drinking water supply and urban-industrial demand in the claimant states, which is why disputes acquire strong political salience and often outlast the tribunals that adjudicate them.
static.whyInNews: A roughly 30-year-old water dispute involving Gujarat has been settled, with Gujarat set to receive water under a new inter-state arrangement.
static.wayForward: Negotiated settlements backed by credible data-sharing, basin-level master planning and institutionalised monitoring tend to be more durable than purely adversarial adjudication. Strengthening river basin organisations and time-bound implementation of awards or agreements would reduce the recurrence of disputes.
keyTerms: Seventh Schedule (Entry 17 State List, Entry 56 Union List)
prelimsPointers: Article 262 allows Parliament to bar the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other courts over inter-state river water disputes.
The ISRWD Act, 1956 was amended in 2002 to provide a negotiation-and-mediation stage and to permit a single tribunal for multiple disputes.
Water supply is a State List subject (Entry 17) while regulation of inter-state rivers and river valleys is a Union List subject (Entry 56).
static.mainsAngle: Examine how Article 262 and the ISRWD Act structure inter-state water dispute resolution, and assess why negotiated settlements are often more durable than tribunal awards.

static.topic: Inter-State Council and Cooperative Federalism
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: The Inter-State Council, provided for under Article 263, is a recommendatory body for inquiring into and advising upon disputes between states and for deliberating on subjects of common interest. It is distinct from the adjudicatory route of water dispute tribunals.
static.background: India's quasi-federal design divides powers through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists in the Seventh Schedule, with residuary powers with the Union (Article 248). The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007) reviewed Centre-State balance and recommended strengthening consultative federal institutions. Cooperative and competitive federalism have since become standard vocabulary in Indian polity debates.
static.whyInNews: The Gujarat water settlement illustrates the negotiated, cooperative route to resolving inter-state resource disputes, complementing the tribunal mechanism.
static.wayForward: Institutionalising regular Inter-State Council and zonal council meetings, and building shared data platforms on water availability, would give negotiated settlements a firmer evidentiary base.
prelimsPointers: The Inter-State Council under Article 263 is a recommendatory body and not a court.
Residuary powers of legislation rest with the Union under Article 248.
static.mainsAngle: Assess the role of consultative federal institutions such as the Inter-State Council in resolving inter-state resource disputes.

static.topic: Counter-insurgency and internal security framework in Jammu and Kashmir
static.syllabusNode: Security — Internal Security
static.whatIsIt: Internal security in J&K is handled through a layered architecture: the J&K Police and its local auxiliaries, central armed police forces, the Army's counter-insurgency grid, and intelligence agencies such as the IB, coordinated by the Ministry of Home Affairs, with legal backing from AFSPA and the UAPA.
static.background: Insurgency in J&K dates to the late 1980s; AFSPA has been in force in notified 'disturbed areas'. The NIA was created in 2008 to investigate terror offences under the NIA Act. The SAMADHAN doctrine guides the counter-left-wing-extremism strategy, and the same development-plus-security logic is often invoked in J&K. The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 reorganised the State into a Union Territory.
static.geography: Kishtwar district lies in the Chenab valley of the Jammu division, a hilly, forested district adjoining Doda, Ramban and Anantnag; such terrain has historically facilitated infiltration and militant hideouts.
static.socioEconomic: The district economy is largely rural and horticulture-based, with significant local dependence on security-related employment, including recruitment as Special Police Officers; youth unemployment and out-migration are recurring local concerns.
static.whyInNews: Allegations that two Special Police Officers were killed by the Army in a mistaken-identity incident in Kishtwar on November 11, followed by a political row and protests.
static.wayForward: Transparent and time-bound inquiries into the conduct of forces, sustained police–public confidence-building, welfare and insurance cover for local recruits such as SPOs, and keeping operational accountability distinct from political rhetoric.
prelimsPointers: The NIA, set up in 2008, investigates terror offences under the NIA Act.
AFSPA empowers designated officers in notified 'disturbed areas' to arrest without warrant and to use force under specified conditions.
static.mainsAngle: Accountability of security forces in counter-insurgency: balancing operational necessity with human rights, local trust and the credibility of official narratives.

static.topic: Police reforms and accountability of security forces
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Police Reforms and Accountability
static.whatIsIt: The accountability framework for police and security forces includes state police acts, Police Complaints Authorities, magisterial and judicial inquiries, the NHRC, and the Supreme Court's directives in Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006).
static.background: In Prakash Singh (2006), the Supreme Court issued directives including constitution of a State Security Commission, a minimum tenure for the DGP, separation of investigation from law and order, a Police Establishment Board, a Police Complaints Authority and a National Security Commission. The Model Police Act, 2006 followed. Police and public order are State List subjects.
static.whyInNews: Competing political claims over the Kishtwar killings have renewed questions about how the conduct of security forces is investigated, reported and publicly communicated.
static.wayForward: Prompt, independent and transparent inquiries with published findings; institutionalised grievance redress for local recruits and affected families; and clear protocols for public communication after contested operations.
keyTerms: Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006)
prelimsPointers: Police and public order are State List subjects under the Seventh Schedule.
Prakash Singh (2006) laid down a set of directives on police reform, including the State Security Commission and Police Complaints Authority.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how institutionalised accountability mechanisms can reconcile counter-insurgency imperatives with the rights and trust of local communities.

prelims: Special Police Officers (SPOs) are locally recruited auxiliary personnel of the J&K Police who assist in counter-insurgency and law-and-order duties.
Kishtwar is a district in the Chenab valley of the Jammu division of Jammu and Kashmir.
The National Investigation Agency (NIA), established in 2008, investigates offences under the NIA Act.
AFSPA applies to areas notified as 'disturbed' and grants special powers to designated security personnel.
stories.mainsQuestion: Contested killings in counter-insurgency operations raise questions of accountability and public trust. Examine the institutional mechanisms available to investigate the conduct of security forces in Jammu and Kashmir, and suggest reforms to make such inquiries credible and timely.

onThisDay.title: Suez Canal inaugurated
onThisDay.description: The Suez Canal was inaugurated in Egypt, linking the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea. It became a vital global maritime trade route and strategic chokepoint.

onThisDay.title: Transistor principles observed
onThisDay.description: American scientists John Bardeen and Walter Houser Brattain observed the basic principles of the transistor. This breakthrough enabled the electronics revolution and modern computing.
onThisDay.upscLink: Science & Technology: semiconductors, electronics, and modern computing.

onThisDay.title: 14th Dalai Lama officially named
onThisDay.description: Lhamo Dondrub was officially named the 14th Dalai Lama. The institution is central to Tibet's religious authority and India-China relations.
onThisDay.upscLink: India-China relations; Tibet issue; international relations.

onThisDay.title: Lunokhod 1 lands on the Moon
onThisDay.description: The Soviet Union landed Lunokhod 1 on Mare Imbrium on the Moon. It was the first remote-controlled rover to land on another world, released by the Luna 17 spacecraft.
onThisDay.upscLink: Space technology: lunar exploration and rover missions.

onThisDay.title: Velvet Revolution begins
onThisDay.description: In Czechoslovakia, a student demonstration in Prague was quelled by riot police, sparking an uprising aimed at overthrowing the communist government. The Velvet Revolution succeeded on December 29.
onThisDay.upscLink: World history: Cold War and collapse of communism in Eastern Europe.
